questions.q: What is a position's "contribution to portfolio return," precisely?
options: The position's own return, regardless of how much capital it received
The position's weight multiplied by its own return over the period
The position's Sharpe ratio multiplied by its weight
The total portfolio return divided by the number of positions
questions.explain: Contribution to return = weight x that position's own return. This is why a high-return position with a tiny allocation can contribute almost nothing, while a modest-return position with a large allocation can dominate the portfolio's result.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked example, the portfolio returned +14.8% overall, but asset AAA contributed -8.5 percentage points on its own. What does this illustrate?
options: The calculation must be wrong, since a portfolio can't have a losing position and a positive total return
A healthy-looking headline portfolio return can fully mask a persistently losing position that another position is bailing out
AAA must have had a negative weight in the portfolio
Contribution to return and total return are always identical for every asset
questions.explain: The headline 14.8% return looked fine, but it masked the fact that one of four positions (AAA) was a consistent drag the whole period, fully offset by a strong contribution from BBB. This is exactly what attribution is designed to surface.

questions.q: Why can an individual asset's percentage share of total portfolio return exceed 100% or be negative?
options: This is always a sign of a calculation error
Because the percentages are shares of a net number (total return), not independent probabilities that must sum to at most 100%
Because weights in a portfolio must always sum to more than 100%
It can only happen if short positions are used
questions.explain: Since one asset's negative contribution is offset by another's positive contribution, the individual percentage shares of the net total can go negative or exceed 100% — they're shares of a net outcome, not mutually exclusive probabilities.

questions.q: What is the practical benefit of attributing performance to "sleeves" (sub-strategies) rather than only to individual assets?
options: It eliminates the need to ever compute attribution at the asset level
It answers whether each signal or sub-strategy is actually earning its capital allocation, which supports ongoing risk-budgeting decisions
It guarantees that each sleeve will continue to perform the same way in the future
Sleeve-level attribution is only possible for single-asset portfolios
questions.explain: Grouping contributions by sleeve answers a research-management question directly: is each signal earning the risk budget it was given, or is one sleeve riding along on another's performance — informing ongoing risk-budgeting decisions from Chapter 2.

questions.q: What is the key limitation of performance attribution, according to the lesson?
options: It cannot be computed without real brokerage data
It tells you where return came from in the sample measured, but doesn't by itself predict whether that pattern will continue — a single period's attribution is an in-sample measurement
It only works for portfolios with exactly two assets
It always overstates the contribution of the best-performing asset
questions.explain: Attribution is diagnostic and historical: it shows where return came from in the period measured. It doesn't guarantee the same sleeve or asset will keep contributing the same way, and over-trusting one period's result repeats the overfitting warning from Lesson 19.
